topics.name: Interactive media and the user experience

dotPoints.description: Investigate how interactive media and the user experience (UX) is used to communicate information to an audience

prompts.question: Outline two features of interactive media that help a website communicate information to its audience.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional council launches a website with flood-warning maps that residents can zoom and filter, river-level graphs and short instructional videos. Many residents check the site on a phone during storms, so the council needs the information to be quick to understand.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines two distinct features of interactive media, each explained in terms of how it helps the audience take in the information, such as zooming a map or a clear menu
2 marks: Outlines one feature of interactive media and links it to communicating information, or names two features with only limited explanation
1 mark: Identifies one feature of interactive media without explaining how it communicates information to the audience
markerNotes: Name two different features, such as zooming, filtering or a clear layout, and say what each does for the reader.
Each feature needs a link to communicating information; a feature with no effect on understanding earns no credit.
A brief outline of one or two sentences per feature is enough for this question.
commonStudentErrors: Listing parts of a website, such as the logo or the colours, without saying how they communicate information.
Describing interactive media in general terms, such as saying it is popular with young people, rather than naming a feature.
Giving the same feature twice in different words, such as 'zoom' and 'magnify'.

sampleAnswers.answer: Interactive media lets residents zoom and filter the flood map, so they can find the streets that matter to them. Clear labels and a consistent layout also support the user experience (UX), helping the audience read the warning quickly on a small phone screen. Together these features communicate information more effectively than a static notice.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two distinct features are outlined, and each is linked to helping the audience understand the warning. The UX point is applied to the phone-based scenario, so full marks are earned.

sampleAnswers.answer: Residents can zoom and filter the flood map, which helps them find their street. The website also has videos, which make it more interesting to visit.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The zoom and filter feature is outlined and linked to communicating information, which earns two marks. The videos are named without any explanation, so the answer does not reach the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: A flood map that residents can zoom into.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A feature is identified, but the answer does not explain how it communicates information to the audience, so one mark is earned.

prompts.question: Explain how the user experience (UX) of a touch-screen exhibit affects how well school students understand the information it is designed to communicate.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional museum installs a touch-screen exhibit about the history of its local river for school groups. The exhibit has a main menu, large buttons, short videos and a timed quiz at the end, and the museum wants students to leave understanding how the river shaped the town.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains how specific features of the user experience (UX), such as menu design and feedback, affect students' ability to follow the interactive media content, with a clear cause and effect for the exhibit
4 marks: Explains how a feature of the user experience affects students' understanding of the content, with a clear link to the exhibit but limited development of the cause and effect
3 marks: Explains one way the user experience affects understanding, with some link to the exhibit, but the explanation is underdeveloped or partly general
2 marks: Identifies a user experience feature of the exhibit and states that it affects students, without explaining how
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported statement about the exhibit or its interactive media
markerNotes: Show the chain from a design feature to what the student does or understands; that cause and effect separates a strong answer from a description.
Use the exhibit in the scenario, such as the menu or the button feedback, rather than discussing user experience in general.
Name the information being communicated so the marker can see that the design choices serve the content.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the exhibit's features, such as its screens and colours, without saying how they affect understanding.
Stating that good UX makes the exhibit 'better' without a cause-and-effect explanation.
Discussing user experience in general terms that could apply to any website, rather than the touch-screen exhibit.

sampleAnswers.answer: The user experience (UX) of the exhibit determines whether students can follow the interactive media content. When the main menu is simple and the buttons are large, students can move straight to the river history and focus on its message. Clear feedback, such as a highlighted button when it is pressed, tells students that their choice has registered, which reduces confusion. Consistent icons and a clear back button also mean students do not have to relearn the controls at each station. If the navigation is cluttered, students spend their time working out the controls instead of reading, so they understand the content less well. Good UX therefore keeps the audience focused on the message, which is how the exhibit can communicate information effectively to its audience.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two user experience features are explained with a clear cause and effect for the students, and the answer stays on the exhibit. The closing point links the design back to communicating information, so full marks are earned.

sampleAnswers.answer: A simple menu helps students use the exhibit, so they can read the river history. Good design makes the exhibit easier to use for everyone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The simple menu is explained with a link to reading the content, but the second sentence is general and not explained for this exhibit, so the answer reaches three marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The exhibit is easy to use, so students learn more.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant statement is made, but it is not supported or linked to how the design affects understanding, so one mark is earned.

dotPoints.description: Investigate social, ethical and legal issues when developing and implementing interactive media systems

prompts.question: Outline one social, one ethical and one legal issue a developer must consider when implementing the quiz app.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a developer is building an interactive quiz app for high school students. The app records each student's answers, shows a class leaderboard with students' names, and sends weekly progress reports to parents through an online platform.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines one social, one ethical and one legal issue, each explained and linked to the quiz app's features and users
3 marks: Outlines all three categories, but one explanation is brief or not linked to the app's features
2 marks: Outlines two of the three categories with explanation, or names all three without explanation
1 mark: Identifies one relevant social, ethical or legal issue without explaining how it applies to the app
markerNotes: Give one social, one ethical and one legal issue as separate categories, since ethics concerns what is fair and legal concerns what the law requires.
Link each issue to the quiz app, such as the leaderboard or the parent reports, rather than naming a general concern.
A legal issue should refer to a real obligation, such as the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), explained in terms of its effect on the app.
commonStudentErrors: Naming two issues in the same category, such as two social issues, and leaving the ethical or legal part blank.
Treating legal compliance and ethical responsibility as the same point, so one issue is counted twice.
Giving a single word such as 'privacy' with no explanation of how the app creates the issue.

sampleAnswers.answer: A social issue is that the class leaderboard may embarrass students who score poorly, so the developer should consider showing results privately. An ethical issue is that the app records every answer, so the developer should collect only the data needed for learning and be open with students and parents about what is kept. A legal issue is that the developer must consider the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), which governs how personal information such as student results is collected, used and disclosed in progress reports. Each consideration shapes how the interactive media systems are designed and who they serve.
sampleAnswers.feedback: All three categories are outlined, and each is explained and linked to the quiz app's features and users. The Privacy Act reference is specific and applied, so full marks are earned.

sampleAnswers.answer: The class leaderboard may embarrass students who score poorly, which is a social issue. The app also records answers, so the developer should think about what data is kept, an ethical issue.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Social and ethical issues are both outlined with explanation, but no legal issue is given, so the answer reaches two marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Privacy is a concern when students use the app.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant issue is identified, but it is not explained or placed in a category, so one mark is earned.

prompts.question: Discuss the trade-off a developer faces when an interactive media system stores detailed student data to personalise feedback.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: the developer of the quiz app wants the system to store each student's pattern of errors so that it can recommend targeted practice. Some teachers support the feature, while some parents and students are concerned about who could see the stored data and how it would be used.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses the trade-off between the benefits of personalised feedback and the social, ethical and legal issues of storing student data, weighing both sides and reaching a reasoned conclusion about the interactive media system
5 marks: Discusses both sides of the trade-off with relevant social, ethical and legal points, but one issue is treated briefly or the conclusion is only partly reasoned
4 marks: Discusses the benefits and at least one concern of storing student data with some reference to the app, but no reasoned conclusion is reached
3 marks: Identifies relevant issues such as privacy or fairness, with limited link to the trade-off or to the app
2 marks: Identifies a benefit or a concern of storing student data, with little development
1 mark: Makes a brief relevant statement about student data with no link to the trade-off
markerNotes: Weigh the benefit against the risk for the same students, rather than listing benefits and risks in separate paragraphs.
Refer to the quiz app and the developer's choice to store error patterns, so the discussion stays on this system.
A reasoned conclusion, such as support with consent and an opt-out, is what lifts a discussion into the top band.
commonStudentErrors: Listing social, ethical and legal issues as separate points with no link between them or to the trade-off.
Saying that collecting data is simply 'bad' without weighing the benefit to students.
Treating a legal obligation as an ethical choice, or the reverse, without explaining the difference.

sampleAnswers.answer: The developer's case for storing error patterns is that personalised feedback can help students improve faster, and teachers may welcome a system that targets practice. However, the student data is personal and could reveal weaknesses that students would prefer to keep private, which is a social concern if classmates or parents can see it. Ethically, the developer must be transparent about what is stored and must not use the data for purposes students did not expect. Legally, privacy law requires the developer to limit collection to what is needed, keep the data secure and use it only for the purpose for which it was collected. The trade-off is justified only if students and parents are informed and can opt out, with informed consent given before any data is stored. On balance, the interactive media system can improve learning without eroding trust, but only under these conditions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both sides of the trade-off are weighed, with social, ethical and legal points each linked to the quiz app. The conclusion is reasoned and conditional, which earns the full six marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Storing error patterns could help students improve, but the student data is personal and could be seen by others. The developer must be transparent about what is stored and collect only what is needed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The benefit and a concern are discussed with some reference to the app, but no reasoned conclusion is reached, so the answer earns four marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Personalised feedback helps students, but the stored data is private, so the developer should be careful.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A benefit and a concern are identified, but neither is developed, so the answer reaches two marks.

dotPoints.description: Research the evolution of interactive media (prevalence of blogs, online video and digital radio; privacy issues and the use of intellectual property, including Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP))

prompts.question: Describe how the growing prevalence of blogs and online video has changed the ways a local history society can share its research.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a local history society has completed a study of its town's early buildings. Its members are deciding whether to publish the findings as a blog, as a short online video series or as a segment on a community digital radio station.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes two distinct ways the growing prevalence of blogs and online video changes how the society shares its research, each linked to a feature of the scenario
3 marks: Describes two ways that blogs or online video change sharing, with one linked to the society's research and the other stated in general terms
2 marks: Describes one way that blogs, online video or digital radio changes how research is shared, with little link to the scenario
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported statement about blogs, online video or digital radio without describing a change
markerNotes: Describe the change itself, such as readers commenting on blog posts or viewers seeing buildings on screen, rather than just naming the format.
Link each change to the society's research, for example the buildings it studied.
Two distinct ways earn credit; the same idea repeated in two wordings earns one mark.
commonStudentErrors: Naming blogs, online video and digital radio without describing how they have changed the way research is shared.
Writing that the internet is 'good' or 'modern' without describing a specific change.
Describing one format in detail and ignoring the others in the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: The growing prevalence of blogs means the society can publish its research as written articles that readers can comment on, which turns the publication into interactive media that invites discussion. Online video lets the society show the buildings visually, so viewers can see architectural details that a written report cannot convey. A community digital radio segment offers a spoken option that reaches listeners who may not read online. Each format reaches a different audience, so the society's choice depends on which community members it wants its research to reach.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two distinct changes are described and each is linked to the society's research and its choice of format. The answer covers the scenario's options well, so full marks are earned.

sampleAnswers.answer: Blogs let the society post research online, so more people can read it. This is easier than printing a report.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One way of sharing is described, but the link to the society's research is brief, so the answer earns two marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Online video is popular, so the society could use it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant statement is made, but it does not describe a change in how research is shared, so one mark is earned.

prompts.question: Assess the privacy and intellectual property risks, including ICIP, of publishing the society's material as an online video series.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: the society's research includes recorded interviews with long-time residents, a family's private photograph collection, and an Aboriginal place name and oral stories about the river, shared with the society by local Traditional Owners. The society wants to publish all of this material as a free online video series.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the privacy, intellectual property and ICIP risks, weighing their seriousness against the benefit of publication and reaching a justified judgement about the video series
5 marks: Assesses at least two risk areas with relevant detail, but ICIP is treated briefly or the judgement is only partly justified
4 marks: Discusses two relevant risks with reasons linked to the scenario, but ICIP is not developed or no judgement is reached
3 marks: Identifies relevant risks such as privacy or copyright, with limited link to the online video series or to the residents and Traditional Owners
2 marks: Identifies one relevant risk of publishing the material, with little development
1 mark: Makes a brief relevant statement about privacy or copyright without linking it to the scenario
markerNotes: Weigh the risks against each other and say which matters most, with reasons; a list of risks alone stays in the middle band.
Recognise that owning a recording does not settle whether cultural knowledge can be shared, which is the core of ICIP.
End with a judgement on whether and under what conditions the series should be published.
commonStudentErrors: Treating privacy, intellectual property and ICIP as the same issue, or using them as synonyms.
Stating that ICIP is just copyright, which misses the cultural rights of the Traditional Owners.
Listing risks without a judgement about whether the society should publish.

sampleAnswers.answer: Privacy is the first risk. The recorded interviews reveal personal information about residents, and the family photographs may show people who never agreed to appear in a public online video. The society should obtain informed consent from each interviewee and check that the family permits publication. Intellectual property is a second risk: the photographs and interview recordings belong to their creators, so the society needs permission before it reproduces them. The most serious risk concerns Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP). The place name and oral stories are cultural knowledge held by the Traditional Owners, so publishing them without their consent could breach ICIP principles even though the society holds the recording. The society should consult the Traditional Owners and remove or defer that material. Overall, the society should not publish the online video series until consent and cultural approval are secured, since the risks to people and to cultural knowledge outweigh the benefit of an early release.
sampleAnswers.feedback: All three risk areas are assessed and weighed, and the most serious risk is identified with reasons. The judgement on publication is clear and conditional, which earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Privacy is a risk because interviewees and families in the photographs may not have agreed to publication. Intellectual property also matters, since the society needs permission to publish photographs it did not take.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two relevant risks are discussed with reasons, but ICIP is not considered and no judgement is reached, so the answer earns four marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Publishing the interviews online could breach residents' privacy, so the society should be careful.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One relevant risk is identified with little development, which earns two marks.

dotPoints.description: Describe the contribution of interactive media systems to a range of enterprises (how simulation, gamification and augmented reality (AR) support online training and learning; how streaming services, gaming and virtual reality (VR) improve access to entertainment; how specialist apps support delivery tracking, advertising and communication)

prompts.question: Demonstrate, with a specific example, how a specialist app can support delivery tracking for a regional courier company.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional courier company wants to improve communication with its customers. It is considering a delivery-tracking app that customers can open on their phones, and an online training module for new drivers.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Demonstrates one clear contribution of an interactive media system to delivery tracking, supported by a specific example from the courier scenario
2 marks: Demonstrates a relevant contribution of an interactive media system, but the example is general or not linked to the courier
1 mark: Identifies a relevant feature of a specialist app without an example or explanation of its contribution
markerNotes: Name the specific contribution, such as tracking or alerts, and show how it changes something for the business or the customer.
The specific example is what earns the top mark; a general statement that apps are useful earns less.
Keep the example tied to the courier company's situation in the scenario.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a specialist app without saying what it contributes to the enterprise.
Describing an app that does not fit the question, such as a game or a streaming service, rather than a delivery-tracking app.
Giving a general example, such as 'apps make things easier', instead of a specific feature for the courier.

sampleAnswers.answer: Specialist apps are interactive media systems that support enterprises. For example, the courier's app sends each customer a notification when the driver is two stops away, which supports delivery tracking and communication between the business and its customers. Customers can prepare for the drop-off, so fewer parcels are missed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One clear contribution to delivery tracking is demonstrated with a specific example from the courier scenario, so full marks are earned.

sampleAnswers.answer: A tracking app shows customers where their parcel is, which helps with communication.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant contribution is shown, but the example is general and is not developed for the courier, so the answer earns two marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Specialist apps can send alerts to customers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant feature is identified, but its contribution is not explained, so one mark is earned.

prompts.question: Analyse how simulation, gamification and augmented reality could support the online training of the courier company's new drivers.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional courier company trains many new drivers each year. Training is currently a classroom course, and many drivers find the safe lifting and loading rules hard to remember. The company is considering an online program that includes a simulated loading dock, points and badges for completed modules, and an augmented reality overlay of safety prompts on real parcels.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how simulation, gamification and augmented reality each support online training, linking every tool to how drivers learn and retain safety rules, and considers a limitation or condition for success
5 marks: Analyses at least two of the tools with clear links to driver learning, but one tool is treated briefly or the limitations are not developed
4 marks: Analyses two tools with some links to training outcomes, but the explanation of how they support learning is partly general
3 marks: Describes the tools and their general purpose, with limited analysis of how they support the courier's online training
2 marks: Identifies one tool and a benefit of online training, with little development
1 mark: Makes a brief relevant statement about gamification or simulation with no link to the courier's training
markerNotes: Analyse by linking each tool to a learning benefit, such as repeated practice or retention, rather than describing what each tool is.
Use the courier scenario, such as safe lifting or loading routines, to ground the analysis.
A limitation, such as cost or the need for accurate simulations, shows the balanced thinking the top band requires.
commonStudentErrors: Defining simulation, gamification and augmented reality without explaining how each supports training.
Claiming the tools will 'definitely' make drivers safer, with no reasoning about how they work.
Writing about streaming or virtual reality entertainment, which is outside this training scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Simulation supports online training by letting new drivers practise loading and delivery routines in a virtual depot without risk to staff or parcels. Each practice run can be repeated until the driver is confident, which builds skill more effectively than a single classroom session. Gamification adds motivation: points and badges for completed modules encourage drivers to finish the program and revisit the safety rules, reinforcing learning over time. Augmented reality extends this by overlaying safety prompts onto a real parcel through a phone camera, so a driver sees the correct lifting method at the moment it is needed. Together, these tools make training interactive and memorable. The main limitation is cost, because the company must produce accurate simulations and test them on the devices drivers actually use, so the benefit depends on careful development. The simulation can also record each driver's errors, so trainers can target coaching at the rules a driver finds hardest.
sampleAnswers.feedback: All three tools are analysed with links to how drivers learn, and the answer weighs a limitation. The analysis is developed and balanced, so full marks are earned.

sampleAnswers.answer: Simulation lets drivers practise routines safely before real deliveries. Gamification with points and badges can motivate drivers to complete their online training, which supports learning, though the benefit may fade.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two tools are analysed with some links to training, but the explanation is partly general and no limitation is considered, so the answer earns four marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Gamification with badges makes the training more fun for drivers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One tool and a benefit are identified, with little development of how it supports learning, so two marks are earned.

dotPoints.description: Evaluate the performance requirements of hardware for specific interactive media projects

prompts.question: Calculate the storage needed for this uncompressed video, in megabytes (MB), where 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes. Show your working and give the answer to one decimal place.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a studio is producing a 10-second product demonstration for a museum display. The video is 1280 pixels wide by 720 pixels high, uses 24-bit colour (3 bytes per pixel) and plays at 30 frames per second. The studio's first draft is uncompressed, so every frame is stored in full.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Calculates the bytes for each frame and then the total for ten seconds at 30 frames per second, and states the storage as 829.4 MB with the working shown
2 marks: Calculates the bytes needed for one frame correctly, but the total for the full clip is missing or incorrect
1 mark: Identifies one correct step, such as the number of pixels in each frame, without completing the calculation
markerNotes: Award the working as well as the answer: pixels per frame, bytes per frame, frames per second, then the total.
Check that bytes are used throughout and that the total is converted using the 1,000,000 bytes per MB stated in the question.
The answer must be 829.4 MB to one decimal place, with units.
commonStudentErrors: Using 24 bits per pixel as 24 bytes, which overstates the storage eightfold.
Calculating the storage for one frame and not multiplying by the frames per second and the ten seconds.
Mixing units, such as using 1,024 x 1,024 bytes per megabyte when the question defines 1 MB as 1,000,000 bytes.

sampleAnswers.answer: Each frame has 1280 by 720 pixels, which is 921,600 pixels in total, and each pixel needs 3 bytes, so one frame needs 2,764,800 bytes. Because the video is uncompressed, every frame is stored in full. At 30 frames per second, one second needs 82,944,000 bytes, so ten seconds need 829,440,000 bytes. The storage needed is 829.4 megabytes (MB).
sampleAnswers.feedback: The pixel count, bytes per frame, frames per second and total are all shown with working and units, so full marks are earned.

sampleAnswers.answer: Each frame has 921,600 pixels at 3 bytes each, so one frame needs 2,764,800 bytes. The full clip would need a much larger total.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The per-frame calculation is correct, but the total for the full clip is missing, so the answer earns two marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The video is 1280 by 720 pixels, so each frame has 921,600 pixels.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One correct intermediate step is shown, but the storage total is not calculated, so one mark is earned.

prompts.question: Justify whether one workstation with the same specification could run both the virtual reality (VR) training simulation and the museum kiosk, using their performance requirements.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a studio must select hardware for two interactive media projects. The first is a virtual reality (VR) training simulation for a mining company, which renders 3D scenes in real time at a frame rate of around 90 frames per second, a common target for comfortable VR. The second is a museum kiosk that plays pre-recorded video with touch-screen menus. The studio has the budget for only one workstation.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies whether one workstation can meet both projects by weighing the graphics, memory and frame rate needs of the simulation against the kiosk's modest demands, and states the conditions for the decision
5 marks: Justifies the decision with relevant hardware reasons for both projects, but one requirement is treated briefly or the conditions are only partly developed
4 marks: Compares the two projects' hardware needs with some reasons, but the justification of the workstation choice is brief
3 marks: Describes the hardware needs of one project with some reference to the other, but the decision is mostly descriptive
2 marks: Identifies a difference in hardware needs between the projects, with little development or link to the workstation choice
1 mark: Makes a brief relevant statement about hardware or frame rate with no link to either project
markerNotes: Justify by weighing each project's requirement against the other, then deciding whether one workstation meets both, with reasons.
Name specific components, such as the graphics card, memory and frame rate, rather than general claims about a powerful computer.
A conditional decision, such as 'only if the graphics card is chosen for the simulation', shows the judgement the top band needs.
commonStudentErrors: Saying both projects need 'a good computer' without naming the components that matter.
Describing the simulation's hardware without comparing it with the kiosk.
Concluding that one workstation is suitable without giving the graphics or memory evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: The virtual reality (VR) simulation has far higher hardware performance requirements than the kiosk. Real-time rendering of three-dimensional scenes needs a powerful graphics card and fast memory, and the frame rate must stay near 90 frames per second or users may experience discomfort. The kiosk plays pre-recorded video, which the processor can decode with modest graphics demand, and its touch menus need little processing. A single workstation could run both only if its graphics card is chosen for the simulation, because an underpowered card would make the VR experience stutter. Memory matters too, since the simulation holds 3D models and textures in RAM while the kiosk needs far less. Given the budget, a workstation specified for the simulation would be more than adequate for the kiosk, so one shared workstation is justified, provided the studio tests the simulation's frame rate before purchase.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both projects are weighed on graphics, memory and frame rate, and the justification states the conditions under which one workstation is suitable. This reasoned, conditional decision earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The VR simulation needs a powerful graphics card and a high frame rate, while the kiosk only plays video. A single workstation could run both if it has a strong enough graphics card, so the choice is reasonable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The two projects' needs are compared and a choice is made, but the justification is brief and the conditions are not developed, so the answer earns four marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The simulation needs more hardware than the kiosk, so it is harder to run.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A difference in requirements is identified, but there is no justification of the workstation choice, so two marks are earned.

dotPoints.description: Explain how interactive media systems can support creative processes (sandbox gaming; social media; digital creative commons)

prompts.question: Describe how sandbox gaming lets the student experiment during the creative process.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a Year 11 student is designing a town for a school project in a sandbox game. Later, the student plans to share the finished town on social media and to add music from a digital creative commons library.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes two distinct ways sandbox gaming supports creative processes, such as low-risk trial and feedback from sharing, each linked to the student's town project
3 marks: Describes two ways a sandbox supports creativity, with one linked to the town project and the other stated in general terms
2 marks: Describes one way the sandbox environment supports experimentation, with little link to the student's project
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported statement about sandbox games or creativity, with no description of how they help
markerNotes: Describe the mechanism, such as undoing a change or testing a layout, rather than saying sandbox games are creative.
Link each mechanism to the student's town project and to the experimenting step of the creative process.
Two different mechanisms earn credit; the same idea in two wordings earns one.
commonStudentErrors: Describing what a sandbox game is without saying how it supports the creative process.
Stating that games are creative or fun without explaining the mechanism that makes them so.
Repeating one idea, such as trying designs, in two different wordings.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sandbox gaming supports the creative process because the student can experiment without penalty: a building can be placed, removed and rebuilt until the town layout works. Immediate visual feedback lets the student test how a design looks before committing to it, which encourages trial and error. Sharing the finished town on social media then invites comments that may prompt further revisions. Because each attempt is low-risk, sandbox gaming encourages iteration rather than a single attempt, and this repeated cycle of testing is central to creative work.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two distinct mechanisms are described, trial without penalty and feedback from sharing, and each is linked to the student's town project. This earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: In a sandbox game, the student can build a town and change it whenever they want. This lets them try ideas.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One way sandbox gaming supports experimentation is described with little link to the project, so the answer earns two marks.

prompts.question: Compare how social media and the digital creative commons support this filmmaker's creative process, including the conditions she must meet.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a Year 11 filmmaker is making a short documentary about her school's garden. She plans to share early cuts on social media to gather feedback, and she wants background music from a digital creative commons library, where creators share music under Creative Commons licences.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Compares how social media and the digital creative commons support different stages of the filmmaker's process, weighing the benefits against licence conditions and feedback risks to reach a reasoned conclusion
5 marks: Compares both resources with relevant reasons, but the licence conditions or feedback risks are treated briefly, or the conclusion is only partly reasoned
4 marks: Compares the two resources with some relevant reasons, but the comparison is mostly descriptive or one resource is developed much less
3 marks: Describes social media and the digital creative commons with some link to the filmmaker, but makes no direct comparison
2 marks: Identifies a benefit of each resource with little development and no comparison
1 mark: Makes a brief relevant statement about social media or creative commons without linking it to the filmmaker
markerNotes: Compare on the same basis, such as how each supports the review stage or the production stage, so that the differences are clear.
Use licence conditions, such as attribution or non-commercial use, as evidence on the creative commons side.
A conclusion about which resource matters at which stage shows the judgement the top band needs.
commonStudentErrors: Describing social media and the creative commons separately, without any direct comparison.
Assuming all creative commons material can be used in any way, without mentioning licence conditions.
Treating feedback from social media as always helpful, without noting that comments can be unhelpful.

sampleAnswers.answer: Social media and the digital creative commons both support the creative process, but at different stages. Social media supports the review stage: sharing early cuts gives the filmmaker rapid feedback from viewers, which lets her test whether scenes hold attention and revise before release. Its value depends on the quality of comments, and public posting can expose unfinished work to criticism. The digital creative commons supports the production stage by providing background music she can use without negotiating a separate licence for each track. However, a Creative Commons licence attaches conditions, such as attribution to the creator, and she must check whether a track allows commercial use if the documentary is later sold. Social media therefore helps her improve the work, while the digital creative commons helps her build it. Both are valuable only if she meets the licence conditions and weighs feedback critically.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The two resources are compared by the stage of the process they support, with the licence conditions and feedback risks weighed. The conclusion is reasoned, which earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Social media gives the filmmaker feedback on early cuts, which helps her revise the documentary. The digital creative commons provides music she can use, but she must follow the licence conditions, such as attribution.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both resources are described with a reason each, but the comparison is brief and no conclusion is reached, so the answer earns four marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Social media lets her share the film and get comments, and creative commons music is free to use.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A benefit of each resource is identified, but there is no comparison, and the claim that creative commons music is free to use ignores its licence conditions, so two marks are earned.

dotPoints.description: Examine how human behaviour may be influenced by interactive media, including opportunities for people with disability to explore and participate in their environment

prompts.question: Describe how captions and a text transcript allow a visitor who is deaf or hard of hearing to explore the exhibits in the online video tour.

markerNotes: Describe how the feature removes a barrier, such as relying on sound, rather than simply naming captions.

A text transcript lets the visitor read at their own pace, and screen readers can read it aloud for people who are blind. Together these features allow people with disability to explore the exhibits and participate in the tour.

prompts.question: Examine how the app may influence residents' walking behaviour, and how its voice navigation allows residents with disability to explore and participate in the trails.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a city council launches a free mobile app that guides residents along its walking trails. The app sends push notifications at set times, counts steps, awards badges for weekly goals and offers voice navigation and high-contrast maps for residents with vision impairment.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Examines how notifications, step counts and badges may influence walking habits, and how voice navigation and high-contrast maps let residents with disability explore and participate, reaching a balanced judgement
5 marks: Examines the influence on behaviour and the access benefits with relevant reasons, but one area is developed less fully or the judgement is only partly reasoned
4 marks: Examines one influence on behaviour and one accessibility feature with some reasoning, but the explanation of either is brief
3 marks: Describes the app's features and their likely effects on residents, with limited examination of how behaviour or access is influenced
2 marks: Identifies one feature of the app and a possible effect, with little development
1 mark: Makes a brief relevant statement about the app or walking with no link to behaviour or disability
markerNotes: Examine by tracing a feature to its likely effect on behaviour, and say where the effect may be limited, such as novelty wearing off.
Treat accessibility as a design feature with an effect on participation, not as an add-on or a separate topic.
Qualify claims about behaviour, since influence is likely rather than certain; the strongest answers say so.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that notifications 'make people exercise' without explaining how the feature works.
Describing voice navigation as useful for everyone, without linking it to residents with vision impairment.
Treating the behaviour and disability parts as separate topics, with no link between them.

sampleAnswers.answer: The app is interactive media that may influence human behaviour through its design. Push notifications prompt residents to walk at set times, and step counts show progress, which can build a regular walking habit. Badges give feedback that reinforces the habit, although the effect may fade once the novelty wears off, so the influence is not guaranteed. The app also affects access. Voice navigation gives turn-by-turn directions, so a resident with vision impairment can follow a trail without relying on a printed map, and high-contrast maps help others with low vision read the route. These features allow people with disability to explore and participate in the trails on equal terms with other residents. Overall, the app's influence on behaviour is positive for many residents, but its benefits depend on accessible design being treated as a core requirement rather than an optional extra.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The behaviour influence and the accessibility benefits are both examined with reasons, and the influence is qualified. The balanced judgement earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Push notifications and step counts may encourage residents to walk regularly, though the effect may fade. Voice navigation lets residents with vision impairment explore the trails without a printed map.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One influence on behaviour and one accessibility feature are explained with some reasoning, but neither is examined in depth, so the answer earns four marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The app's rewards may make people walk more, and voice navigation helps some residents.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One feature and a possible effect are identified with little development, so two marks are earned.

dotPoints.description: Investigate how digital marketing techniques influence consumer behaviour (guided choice (nudging); default settings, including cookies; autofill; pop-ups promoting online shopping)

prompts.question: Clarify how the pre-ticked 'send me offers' box can influence a customer's decision to receive marketing emails.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: an online clothing store's checkout page has the 'send me offers' box already ticked. Many customers complete the purchase without changing this box, and the store then sends them marketing emails for the following year.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Clarifies how the pre-ticked default influences consumer behaviour through inertia and nudging, linking the effect to the store's digital marketing and to the customer's informed consent
3 marks: Clarifies the influence of the default setting on consumer behaviour with a clear link to the store, but the explanation of inertia or consent is brief
2 marks: Clarifies one effect of the pre-ticked box on customers, with limited explanation of why it works
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported statement about digital marketing or default settings without clarifying the effect
markerNotes: Explain why the default works, such as customers not changing settings, rather than only naming the technique.
Link the default to the store's digital marketing aim, such as a larger mailing list.
An ethical point about informed consent shows the wider effect on the customer, which the top band expects.
commonStudentErrors: Naming 'default settings' or 'nudging' without clarifying how the pre-ticked box changes a decision.
Writing that the box 'forces' customers to accept, when the customer can untick it.
Confusing a default setting with a pop-up, which is a separate technique.

sampleAnswers.answer: Default settings are options that are already selected before the customer acts. The pre-ticked box influences consumer behaviour through inertia, because many customers do not change a setting, so they receive marketing emails they did not actively request. The store benefits from this digital marketing technique, since the default creates a larger mailing list without extra effort. The effect is a nudge towards accepting, which is why the default should be unticked if the customer's informed consent is to be genuine.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The pre-ticked default is clarified through inertia and nudging, and the answer links it to the store's digital marketing and to informed consent. This earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The box is already ticked, so many customers will leave it as it is and receive emails.

sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant statement is made, but it does not clarify how the box influences decisions, so one mark is earned.

prompts.question: Analyse how the store's combined use of autofill, cookies and pop-ups may influence this customer's purchasing decision.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a customer returns to an online shoe store on her phone. The store has saved her card details through autofill, and cookies show she browsed running shoes last week. A pop-up offering a limited-time discount appears just as she reaches the checkout.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how autofill, cookies and pop-ups each influence the purchasing decision, linking each mechanism to the customer's behaviour and weighing the ethical risks of the combined approach
5 marks: Analyses at least two mechanisms with clear links to the purchase, but cookies or the ethical risks are treated briefly
4 marks: Analyses two techniques with some relevant links to consumer behaviour, but the explanation is partly general and the ethical risk is not considered
3 marks: Describes the techniques and a likely effect on the customer, with limited analysis of the mechanism behind the effect
2 marks: Identifies a technique and a benefit to the customer or store, with little analysis of how it influences the decision
1 mark: Makes a brief relevant statement about online shopping or pop-ups with no link to consumer behaviour
markerNotes: Analyse the mechanism for each technique, such as removing effort or creating urgency, before judging how far it influences the purchase.
Link cookies to the pop-up, since the scenario uses browsing history to target the offer.
An ethical judgement, such as the need for disclosure or an easy opt-out, separates the top band from a description.
commonStudentErrors: Describing autofill, cookies and pop-ups as techniques without analysing how each changes the purchase.
Treating cookies as passwords or as a virus, rather than as small files that store browsing data.
Assuming every customer responds to pop-ups in the same way, without qualifying the influence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Autofill and pop-ups influence consumer behaviour through different mechanisms. Autofill removes the effort of entering card details, so the customer completes the purchase in fewer steps, and each removed step makes a purchase more likely. Pop-ups create urgency: a limited-time discount invites a decision before the customer has compared prices. Cookies support the approach by recording browsing history, so the store can match the pop-up to the running shoes she has already viewed. This digital marketing combination is effective because it reduces the time and deliberation the customer would otherwise spend. However, it also raises concerns. The customer may buy on impulse, and her browsing data is used in ways she may not expect, so the store should disclose its use of cookies and make it easy to decline. An ethical store would balance this commercial gain against the customer's ability to make an informed choice, and would avoid using stored data in ways that feel intrusive.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Each mechanism is analysed in terms of its effect on the purchase, and the ethical risks of the combined approach are weighed. This earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pop-ups create urgency with a limited-time discount, so the customer may decide quickly. Autofill makes checkout faster by filling in card details, which reduces effort.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two techniques are analysed with some links to the purchase, but the explanation is partly general and the ethical risk is not considered, so the answer earns four marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Autofill saves time, and pop-ups can offer discounts to customers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A technique and a benefit are identified, with little analysis of how they influence the decision, so two marks are earned.

dotPoints.description: Evaluate social media applications that encourage human connections (crowdsourcing through a social media app; learning via massive online open courses (MOOCs); gaming platforms that encourage massive multiplayer online games (MMOGs))

prompts.question: Classify each platform as crowdsourcing, a massive online open course (MOOC) or a massive multiplayer online game (MMOG), and give one feature that supports each classification.

markerNotes: Check each category against its defining feature: contributions from many people, open enrolment for large numbers, or persistent play for many players at once.

Giving a category without any feature that supports it.

prompts.question: Evaluate how effectively the three options build human connections among the students.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a high school is deciding how to help students connect with their community and with each other. The three options are a crowdsourcing app built into the school's social media page for a community-history project, a free online course with thousands of enrolled learners, and a team-based game in which students cooperate in a persistent online world. Teachers are concerned about cyber safety, the accuracy of content and whether online connections are meaningful.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Evaluates the three options against the goal of human connections, weighing the benefits and risks of each and reaching a supported judgement about which is most effective
5 marks: Evaluates at least two options with relevant benefits and risks, but one option or the judgement is treated less fully
4 marks: Evaluates two options with some reasons, but the risks are not weighed against connection benefits or the judgement is missing
3 marks: Describes the three options and their connection benefits, with limited evaluation of how effective each would be
2 marks: Identifies one option with a benefit or a risk, with little development
1 mark: Makes a brief relevant statement about online platforms with no link to human connections
markerNotes: Evaluate by weighing each option's benefit for connection against its risks, then judging which is most effective and why.
Refer to the school's goal of building connection, so the judgement answers the question rather than discussing social media in general.
Name the feature that creates each connection, such as team play, forum discussion or contributions to a shared map.
commonStudentErrors: Describing each option without judging how effective it is at building human connections.
Assuming online connections are always weaker or stronger than face-to-face ones, without evidence.
Ignoring risks, such as cyber safety or inaccurate content, when evaluating.

sampleAnswers.answer: A crowdsourcing app creates human connections between students and community members, who supply and check local information together. Its effectiveness depends on moderation, because open contributions on social media may include inaccurate content and unkind comments. Massive online open courses offer content that is often developed by universities and let students learn at their own pace, but they often provide weak human connections, since interaction is mostly through forums with thousands of other learners. Massive multiplayer online games encourage strong connections, because teams cooperate in real time and friendships can continue offline. However, these games carry cyber safety risks and may distract from learning if they are not structured. On balance, the crowdsourcing option is most effective for community connection if it is moderated, the game is best for teamwork if supervised, and the course is strongest for content but weakest for connection.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Each option is weighed by its connection benefits and risks, and the answer reaches a supported judgement about which is most effective. This earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A crowdsourcing app connects students with community members, which builds communication skills. However, the content may be inaccurate without moderation. Massive multiplayer online games encourage teamwork, though they raise cyber safety concerns.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two options are evaluated with brief reasons and risks, but the courses are not assessed and no judgement is reached, so the answer earns four marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The game is fun and helps students make friends, but it might be unsafe.
