Stating that high-risk simulators are better or more advanced, without giving a reason.
Treating data modelling and automation as the same thing as simulation.

sampleAnswers.answer: In education and training, simulation lets learners practise skills and decisions repeatedly, with immediate feedback and no risk to people or equipment. In high-risk applications such as a chemical plant, simulation rehearses rare but dangerous faults that cannot be tested on the real plant. Both uses rely on data modelling of how the system behaves, and both may use automation to score responses or trigger scenarios. They differ in purpose, however. Training aims to build an operator's competence over time, whereas a plant simulator may also test new shutdown procedures before they are used. That difference matters for fidelity: a training simulator needs to teach the right responses, while a high-risk simulator must reproduce the plant's behaviour accurately enough to trust its results. Both share the aim of safe practice, but the level of accuracy demanded is greater in high-risk applications.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer identifies a shared feature and a clear difference in purpose, uses the chemical plant example to justify the high-risk side, and explains why the accuracy demanded differs.

sampleAnswers.answer: Simulation in training lets learners practise safely, while in a chemical plant it lets staff rehearse dangerous faults. Both use data modelling, but training builds skills, and the plant simulator tests procedures.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both settings are described and linked through data modelling, but the comparison is implied rather than developed, which limits it to the middle band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Simulation is used in training and in dangerous industries.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant but unsupported statement is made. Name one shared feature and one difference, each with an example.

dotPoints.description: Explain the role of intelligent systems in surveillance (closed circuit television (CCTV); biometric scanning; customer loyalty schemes; fraud prevention; sniffing; trolling)

prompts.question: Identify two ways an intelligent system can enhance traditional CCTV surveillance.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A shopping centre is upgrading its security camera system so that staff can respond to incidents faster. The centre's control room currently has one operator watching many screens at the same time.
markerNotes: An enhancement must go beyond recording: the system analyses video automatically, so name what it detects or recognises and what it does with the footage.
Keep the two enhancements distinct: identifying people (who) and detecting unusual events (what is happening).
Describe the output, such as an alert or a match, that helps staff act.
commonStudentErrors: Describing better camera quality or more cameras, which are hardware upgrades rather than intelligent-system enhancements.
Naming 'AI' or 'machine learning' without saying what the system detects or recognises.
Giving two versions of the same feature, such as two kinds of face matching, which counts as one enhancement.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies two distinct enhancements (for example, automated facial recognition to flag people of interest, and anomaly detection to alert staff to unusual behaviour or objects), each with a brief statement of what the system does with the footage
1 mark: Identifies one enhancement with a brief explanation, or names two enhancements without explaining them

sampleAnswers.answer: An intelligent system can enhance CCTV surveillance by adding facial recognition to identify people of interest, and by using anomaly detection to send automated alerts to staff about unusual behaviour, such as an abandoned package.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: two distinct enhancements are named, and each is linked to what the system does with the footage, such as matching a face or alerting staff to unusual behaviour. Keep each description to one clause, as this is a two-mark question.

sampleAnswers.answer: Facial recognition is a feature that a CCTV camera can have.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One enhancement is named, but the answer does not say what the system does with the footage and gives no second enhancement. Add a second intelligent feature, such as anomaly detection, and state what it alerts staff to.

prompts.question: Explain how a bank uses intelligent systems for fraud prevention when a customer uses their credit card.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A cardholder who usually spends in her local area makes an unusually large online purchase from an overseas retailer. The bank's intelligent system flags the transaction and sends a verification message to her phone.
markerNotes: Explain the two stages: building a profile of normal behaviour from past transactions, then assessing each new transaction against it in real time.
Name the factors compared (amount, location, merchant, timing) and show how a deviation is treated as an anomaly.
The automated response (block, hold or verification alert) completes the explanation and should link back to the scenario.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the bank 'checks for fraud' without explaining what the system compares or how it decides.
Describing a fraud analyst reviewing every transaction by hand, which is not an intelligent-system explanation.
Treating every large purchase as fraud, without the profile comparison and risk score that decide it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains both stages clearly: the system builds a profile of the customer's normal spending (amounts, locations, merchants, timing) from past transactions, then assesses each new transaction in real time against that profile, flagging a deviation and triggering an automated response such as a block or verification alert. Links the explanation to the scenario
3 marks: Explains both stages, with the automated response or the scenario link less developed
2 marks: Explains one stage clearly, or describes both stages in general terms
1 mark: Names fraud detection or a feature, such as 'patterns', without explaining how it works

sampleAnswers.answer:
A bank's intelligent system for fraud prevention builds a spending profile for each customer from past transactions, covering usual amounts, locations, merchants and times of purchase. This profile is the baseline for transaction monitoring of the customer's credit card.

When the customer attempts a new transaction, the system assesses it in real time against that profile. A large purchase from a new overseas website deviates sharply from the norm, so anomaly detection flags it. The system then assigns a risk score, and if the score passes a set threshold, it can decline the transaction and send a verification alert to the customer's phone, stopping the fraud before it completes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer explains both stages, the profile of normal behaviour and the real-time comparison, and links the deviation to the overseas purchase and the automated response. Naming the factors compared keeps it an explanation rather than a description.

sampleAnswers.answer: The bank uses a computer system that learns what a customer normally spends. When a new purchase is made, the system checks it against this, and if it looks unusual, it alerts the bank or the customer.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The profile and the check are described in general terms, but the answer does not say which factors are compared (amount, location, merchant) or how a flagged transaction is treated. Name the factors and describe the automated response in the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: The bank uses intelligent systems to stop fraud on credit cards.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This restates the purpose of the system without explaining how it works. Describe the customer profile the system builds and how it checks a new transaction against it.

dotPoints.description: Explain how AI supports efficiency in an IoT network

prompts.question: Outline three ways an AI component could improve efficiency in the building's IoT network, stating the sensor-based outcome for each.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a city council is retrofitting a 12-storey office building with about 1,500 IoT sensors that measure occupancy, temperature, energy use and lift performance. The council wants to cut energy use and reduce unplanned lift breakdowns.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines three distinct ways AI improves efficiency in the building's IoT network, such as learned occupancy control, predictive maintenance and local processing, each linked to a specific sensor-based outcome
2 marks: Outlines two ways AI improves efficiency in the network, with a brief link to a sensor or an outcome for at least one
1 mark: States one general benefit of AI without linking it to the IoT network
markerNotes: Each way needs a sensor-based outcome, such as lights switched off by occupancy readings, not just a general benefit of AI.
Distinct ways, such as occupancy control, predictive maintenance and local processing, score better than three versions of the same energy saving.
Use the building's sensors in the scenario to make each outcome concrete.
commonStudentErrors: Giving three versions of the same idea, such as saving energy in two different ways, as separate points.
Stating a general benefit such as 'AI is smart' without describing how it improves efficiency.
Confusing AI with the sensors themselves, which collect data but do not decide anything.

sampleAnswers.answer: AI can learn occupancy patterns from sensor readings, so heating and lighting on empty floors are reduced, improving energy efficiency across the IoT network. Machine learning models can also predict when a lift motor will need service, so repairs happen before breakdowns, which is predictive maintenance. Processing sensor data at a local gateway lets the building respond quickly without sending every reading to the cloud.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Three distinct ways are outlined, each with a sensor-based outcome, and the energy and lift goals of the scenario are both addressed.

sampleAnswers.answer: AI can use occupancy sensors to switch off lights in empty rooms. It can also predict when equipment needs repair.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two ways AI improves efficiency are outlined with a sensor link for one of them, but the third way is missing, so the answer earns the middle band.

sampleAnswers.answer: AI can make the building use less energy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One general benefit of AI is stated, with no link to the IoT network or to a sensor-based outcome.

prompts.question: Justify whether the council should run its AI models on local edge gateways or in a cloud service, given that the building's heating and lighting control must keep working during an internet outage.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: sensors on each floor send readings to a local gateway, which forwards data to a cloud service. The council has a limited budget for new equipment and wants heating and lighting to keep running if the building loses its internet link.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies a clear recommendation between edge and cloud AI processing, weighing latency, resilience during an outage and budget, and supports each point with specific reasons linked to the building's heating and lighting control
5 marks: Justifies a recommendation with reasons that weigh at least two factors, such as resilience and cost, but one factor is only briefly considered
4 marks: Justifies a choice with a relevant reason linked to the outage requirement, but does not weigh the alternative or the budget
3 marks: Explains one advantage of edge or cloud processing for the building, without reaching a recommendation
2 marks: Describes edge or cloud processing in general terms, with no link to the outage requirement
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported statement about AI processing
markerNotes: A justification needs a recommendation first, then reasons that weigh the alternative, not a description of both options.
The outage requirement in the scenario decides much of the case, so link the reasoning to it.
Mentioning the budget and the existing gateways shows the judgement is based on the scenario.
commonStudentErrors: Describing edge computing and cloud services without reaching a recommendation.
Recommending the cloud because it has more computing power, without addressing the outage requirement.
Treating latency as a minor point when the scenario requires control to continue during an outage.

sampleAnswers.answer: Running the AI models on local edge gateways is the stronger choice for heating and lighting control across the IoT network. Edge computing processes sensor readings where they are produced, so a decision such as dimming a floor's lights takes effect with little latency and keeps working during an internet outage. A cloud service has greater computing power and can train models on data from many buildings, but every live decision would then depend on the internet link and the delay of a round trip. The council's budget also favours local processing, because the gateways already exist on each floor and only the models need installing. The cloud should still hold the historical data, so that models can be retrained periodically and efficiency gains tracked over time. Keeping live control at the edge, with the cloud used for training and reporting, gives the building both resilience and efficiency, which is why the council should adopt it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer makes a clear recommendation, weighs latency, resilience and budget against the cloud option, and ties each reason to the outage requirement.

sampleAnswers.answer: A local gateway keeps heating and lighting working during an outage, while the cloud is useful for storing history. The council should use the gateway for live control, because the cloud depends on the internet link.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer explains the advantage of local processing for the outage requirement, but it does not weigh the budget or the cloud option in any depth.

sampleAnswers.answer: A cloud service could store the building's data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant point is made about the cloud, with no justification of either option and no link to the outage requirement.

dotPoints.description: Develop a set of rules and facts that could be used within an expert system to draw conclusions

prompts.question: State one fact and one IF-THEN rule that a simple expert system designed to recommend a pet could use.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A pet adoption service is building a 'Perfect Pet Finder' expert system. The system asks customers about their home and lifestyle, and its knowledge base must contain the facts and rules that turn those answers into a recommendation.
markerNotes: A fact states something true about the domain, such as a breed's exercise needs. A rule has a testable IF condition and a THEN conclusion.
Use variables the system can check, such as home type or daily exercise time, so that the inference engine can apply the rule.
The fact should support the rule's conclusion, so that the two pieces of knowledge link together.
commonStudentErrors: Writing a conclusion as a fact, such as 'The customer should get a dog', rather than a statement of knowledge about the domain.
Writing a circular or vague rule, such as 'IF the customer wants a pet THEN recommend a pet'.
Using programming syntax such as '!=' without explaining the variables it compares.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Provides one valid fact about a pet and one IF-THEN rule with a specific, testable condition that leads to a recommendation, with the rule linked to the fact
1 mark: Provides a valid fact or a valid IF-THEN rule, but not both, or a rule with no meaningful condition

sampleAnswers.answer:
This expert system holds rules and facts in its knowledge base:
**Fact:** Labradors need at least one hour of exercise every day.
**IF-THEN rule:** IF home_type = 'apartment' AND daily_exercise_minutes < 60 THEN do NOT recommend a Labrador.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the fact is accurate and the rule has two testable conditions that use it, so the knowledge base can draw a conclusion. The answer is precise without being long, which suits a two-mark question.

sampleAnswers.answer:
**Fact:** Dogs are a type of pet.
**Rule:** IF the customer wants a pet THEN recommend a pet.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The fact is valid but general, and the rule is circular: its condition does not narrow the choice. Write a rule with a specific condition about the customer, such as home type or time for exercise, that leads to a clear recommendation.

prompts.question: Construct a set of at least three IF-THEN rules and any necessary facts for an expert system that provides basic technical support for a home Wi-Fi network.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: An internet service provider wants an online troubleshooting tool for customers whose home Wi-Fi is not working. The tool asks yes-or-no questions about the modem and router, then suggests the next step, escalating to a technician only when simple checks fail.
markerNotes: The set should form a diagnostic sequence: simple, cheap checks first, then escalation to a technician.
Each condition should be a variable the user can answer (on or off, yes or no), and each THEN should be a clear, actionable suggestion.
State the facts the rules depend on, such as what the router's lights indicate, so the knowledge base is complete.
commonStudentErrors: Writing a vague condition, such as 'IF the Wi-Fi is bad THEN fix it', that the system cannot test.
Placing the escalation rule before the simple checks, so the sequence does not reflect a logical diagnosis.
Repeating the same condition and conclusion in every rule, so the set adds nothing new.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Constructs a coherent set of at least three IF-THEN rules, supported by the facts they use, with testable conditions and a logical diagnostic sequence from simple checks to escalation. Each conclusion is a clear, actionable suggestion, and the set is internally consistent
3 marks: Constructs three valid rules with a reasonable diagnostic order, but one condition is vague or the facts are missing or unclear
2 marks: Constructs two valid IF-THEN rules, or three rules where most conditions cannot be tested, with little logical sequence
1 mark: Provides one valid IF-THEN rule, or facts without any rules

sampleAnswers.answer:
This expert system holds facts and IF-THEN rules in its knowledge base, and its inference engine applies them when troubleshooting a home Wi-Fi network.

**Facts:** Each light is on or off. A restart clears temporary faults, and line status can be checked remotely.

**Rule 1:** IF power_light = 'off' THEN suggest 'Plug the router into a power outlet.'
**Rule 2:** IF power_light = 'on' AND internet_light = 'off' AND restarted = 'no' THEN suggest 'Unplug the router for 30 seconds.'
**Rule 3:** IF internet_light = 'off' AND restarted = 'yes' AND line_status = 'fault' THEN suggest 'Report a line fault to the provider.'
**Rule 4:** IF internet_light = 'on' AND devices_connect = 'no' THEN suggest 'Check the Wi-Fi password.'
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the rules form a diagnostic sequence, supported by stated facts and conditions the user can answer. Each rule ends in a specific action, and escalation depends on checked conditions (restart done, line status), which is what makes the set coherent.

sampleAnswers.answer: Rule 1: IF internet_light = 'off' THEN suggest 'Restart the router'. Rule 2: IF devices_connect = 'no' THEN suggest 'Check the Wi-Fi password'. Rule 3: IF the problem still exists THEN suggest 'Contact the provider'.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two rules are valid, but the third condition ('the problem still exists') cannot be tested and no facts support it, so the set does not form a clear diagnostic process. Replace it with a checkable variable, such as whether the restart has been done, and state the facts the rules use.

sampleAnswers.answer: Facts: The router has a power light and an internet light. Restarting the router can fix some problems.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Facts are given, but no IF-THEN rule is written, so the system cannot draw any conclusion. Write rules that link a checkable condition, such as the internet light being off, to a suggested action.

dotPoints.description: Apply certainty factors to construct a decision tree for a proposed expert system

prompts.question: Calculate the combined certainty factor for a diagnosis supported by two rules that both lead to the same conclusion, where Rule 1 gives a certainty factor (CF) of 0.6 and Rule 2 gives a CF of 0.5, both positive. Show your working.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a computer repair business is building an expert system that diagnoses why a laptop will not start. Two independent rules both point to a failed power adapter, and the technician must decide how strongly to believe that diagnosis.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Calculates the combined CF correctly using the formula for two positive certainty factors, substituting both values and showing each step to reach 0.8
2 marks: Reaches the correct combined CF of 0.8 with incomplete working, or states the correct formula without completing the calculation
1 mark: Identifies that the two certainty factors must be combined, with no correct calculation
markerNotes: Show the formula, each substitution and the result; a final answer alone earns little.
Two positive certainty factors are combined with CF1 + CF2 × (1 − CF1), not simply added, so the result stays at or below 1.
Linking the result back to the diagnosis shows how the expert system would use it.
commonStudentErrors: Adding the two values to get 1.1, which is above the maximum CF of 1 and so cannot be right.
Multiplying the two values to get 0.3 without using the combining formula.
Giving 0.8 without any working when the question asks for working.

sampleAnswers.answer: The combined certainty factor is CF(combined) = CF1 + CF2 × (1 − CF1). Substituting Rule 1 (0.6) and Rule 2 (0.5) gives 0.6 + 0.5 × (1 − 0.6) = 0.6 + 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.6 + 0.2 = 0.8. Both rules support the power adapter diagnosis, so the decision tree in the expert system should record a combined certainty factor of 0.8 for it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The formula is stated, both values are substituted, and each step leads to 0.8, which gives full working marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The combined CF is 0.8, because both rules support the same diagnosis and their values are combined rather than simply added.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The correct value of 0.8 is reached, but the formula and the steps are not shown, so the answer cannot earn full working marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The two rules should be combined rather than added together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The correct principle is identified, but no calculation is made. Apply the combining formula to the two values.

prompts.question: Analyse how an uncertain answer at the top of a decision tree affects the certainty of conclusions reached further down the tree, using a simple two-rule example.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: the expert system starts by asking whether the laptop's power light is on. The technician can answer only 'probably yes', which the system records as a certainty factor of 0.7; this answer is the premise of the first rule. That rule has a CF of 0.9, and a second rule has a CF of 0.8.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how each certainty factor passes down the tree by multiplying the premise and rule values, calculates the compounding effect across two or more rules, and draws a justified implication for designing the expert system
5 marks: Analyses the propagation of certainty through the tree with correct values for at least two rules, and explains the compounding effect, with a limited implication for the system design
4 marks: Explains that the certainty of a later conclusion depends on earlier answers, with one correct calculation, but the compounding effect is not fully developed
3 marks: Explains that uncertain early answers reduce confidence in later conclusions, without a correct calculation
2 marks: Describes certainty factors in general terms, with no link to the decision tree's structure
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported statement about certainty factors
markerNotes: A conclusion's CF is the premise's CF multiplied by the rule's CF, so the value falls at each step rather than being restated.
Show at least one calculation, because the analysis is strongest when it uses the tree's own values.
The implication for design, such as confirming uncertain early answers, separates a high analysis from a description.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the final conclusion is as certain as the rule that produced it, and ignoring the premise's CF.
Adding the CFs along the tree instead of multiplying them.
Describing what a decision tree is without tracing how the certainty changes.

sampleAnswers.answer: Each conclusion in a decision tree depends on the answers before it, so its certainty can be no higher than the certainty of its premise. Here the first answer, that the power light is 'probably on', has a certainty factor of 0.7. The rule IF the power light is on THEN the power supply is delivering power has a CF of 0.9, so that conclusion has a CF of 0.7 × 0.9 = 0.63. A second rule, IF the power supply is delivering power THEN the charger is not the fault, has a CF of 0.8, so its conclusion is 0.63 × 0.8 = 0.504. The uncertainty compounds down the tree: two rules that each look reliable leave the final conclusion at a CF of only about 0.5. The analysis shows that the expert system should confirm uncertain early answers, such as asking the technician to recheck the light, before drawing conclusions lower down the tree.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer traces the certainty through two rules with correct values, explains the compounding effect, and draws a design implication from it.

sampleAnswers.answer: If the light is only probably on (CF 0.7), a rule with CF 0.9 gives a lower CF of 0.63 for the next conclusion, so the tree is less certain than either value alone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A correct calculation shows the certainty falling down the tree, but the answer does not go on to the second rule or to a design implication.

sampleAnswers.answer: Lower certainty early in the tree makes later answers less certain.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant point is made, but it is not supported by a calculation or an example from the tree.

dotPoints.description: Verify the sources of data used in a decision support system

prompts.question: Clarify the difference between primary data and secondary data for the café's decision support system, giving one example of each.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional café chain uses a decision support system to decide how much coffee and milk to order each week. Its data comes from its own point-of-sale records, a weather forecast from a website and a supplier's published price list.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Clarifies the difference between primary data, collected directly for a purpose, and secondary data, collected by another party, giving a correct example of each from the café's decision support system
2 marks: Clarifies the difference between primary and secondary data in general terms, with one correct example
1 mark: Names primary or secondary data, or gives a distinction with no example
markerNotes: Clarify means making the distinction clear: who collected the data and for what purpose.
An example from the café's system, such as point-of-sale records or a supplier price list, is needed for the top band.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that primary data is more accurate than secondary data, without a reason.
Giving the examples without saying who collected the data.
Confusing primary data with raw data, which is a different distinction.

sampleAnswers.answer: Primary data is collected directly by the user for its own purpose, such as the café's point-of-sale records of coffee and milk sales. Secondary data was collected by someone else, such as a supplier's published price list. The café knows how its own records were collected, but must check the date and origin of a secondary data source before the decision support system relies on it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both kinds of data are distinguished by who collected them and why, and each has a correct example from the café's system.

sampleAnswers.answer: Primary data is collected by the user, such as its own sales records. Secondary data is collected by someone else.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The distinction is correct and one example is given, but the explanation is general, which earns the middle band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Primary data is created by the business itself.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A distinction is named with no example and no reference to the decision support system.

prompts.question: Evaluate the risk of basing the weekly coffee order on a weather forecast from an unverified free website, and judge how much checking the café should do before the decision support system uses it.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a café chain's decision support system uses a free weather website's forecast to adjust the weekly coffee order. Staff have noticed that the site does not name its forecast provider or say when each forecast was last updated.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Evaluates the risk of using the unverified forecast for the order, judging how much verification is needed by weighing the source's unknown provenance, the consequences of error and the checks available, and reaching a supported conclusion
5 marks: Evaluates the risk to the order and identifies sound verification steps, such as checking the forecast against a second source, with a reasoned judgement that is only briefly developed
4 marks: Discusses the risk of an inaccurate forecast and at least one verification step, linked to the coffee order, but without a clear judgement of how much checking is needed
3 marks: Identifies one risk of an unverified forecast with a brief link to the coffee order, but no verification step
2 marks: Describes the forecast or the decision support system in general terms, with no link to verification
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported statement about data sources
markerNotes: Evaluate needs a judgement on how much checking is needed, weighed against the cost of a wrong order.
Name specific verification steps, such as comparing a second source or checking the date, rather than 'check the data'.
The best answers recognise that the source's provenance is unknown, which is the core of verifying a data source.
commonStudentErrors: Accepting the free forecast because the decision support system produces the order, treating the system as the source of truth.
Recommending that the café 'check the forecast' without saying how.
Judging every forecast as equally risky, without matching the checking to the size of the order change.

sampleAnswers.answer: Basing the weekly order on an unverified free forecast carries a real risk, because the decision support system treats the weather forecast as fact. If the forecast is wrong, for example predicting rain on a sunny weekend, the system may cut the order and leave cafés short of coffee on a busy day. A free website may not state who produced its forecast, how old it is or which area it covers, so the café cannot judge its reliability. Before each order, the café should verify the data source by comparing the forecast with a second, established provider, checking the date and location, and recording how often the forecast has matched the actual weather. The amount of checking should match the risk: a forecast that changes the order slightly needs a quick comparison, while one that would cut stock for a major event needs more care. On balance, the forecast should be used only after it has been verified, because the cost of a wrong order exceeds the effort of checking.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer judges the risk from the unknown provenance of the forecast, names specific verification steps, and matches the amount of checking to the size of the risk.

sampleAnswers.answer: A free forecast may be wrong, and the decision support system will treat it as correct. The café should compare it with a second source before ordering, so the order is not cut for the wrong weather.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One risk is identified with a verification step, linked to the coffee order, but the answer does not judge how much checking is needed.

sampleAnswers.answer: The forecast might be wrong, so it should be checked.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant but unsupported statement is made. Explain why the forecast might be wrong and what checking would involve.

dotPoints.description: Use a flowchart to develop a knowledge base of IF-THEN rules to be used by an expert system

prompts.question: Construct a flowchart with three decision diamonds for this repair diagnosis, then write the IF-THEN rule that each route to a recommendation represents.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a home-appliance repair shop wants an expert system that advises whether a washing machine should be repaired or replaced. Staff have given three questions: is the machine less than five years old, is the repair quote below half the replacement price, and does the machine leak water?
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Constructs a coherent flowchart with three decision diamonds in a logical order, and writes an accurate IF-THEN rule for each route to a recommendation, using the scenario's values
3 marks: Constructs a flowchart with the three decisions in a sensible order and IF-THEN rules for most routes, but one route or rule is incomplete or unclear
2 marks: Constructs a partial flowchart or writes one or two IF-THEN rules, with a correct link to the recommendation
1 mark: Identifies one decision or rule relevant to the repair question, without a flowchart
markerNotes: A flowchart needs a decision diamond for each question, with labelled Yes and No branches that lead to a recommendation.
Each IF-THEN rule should use the scenario's own values, such as five years, and combine conditions with AND.
Rules should be mutually exclusive, so that each machine follows only one route.
commonStudentErrors: Drawing decision diamonds with only one branch, so some machines have no route to a recommendation.
Writing vague conditions such as 'if the machine is old', which the system cannot test.
Writing rules that give two different recommendations for the same machine.

sampleAnswers.answer: The flowchart has three decisions: age, repair quote and leaks. Each route gives one IF-THEN rule. IF the machine is five years old or more THEN the recommendation is replacement. IF the machine is under five years old AND the quote is at least half the price THEN the recommendation is replacement. IF the machine is under five years old AND the quote is below half the price AND it leaks THEN the recommendation is repair with a seal check. IF the machine is under five years old AND the quote is below half the price AND it does not leak THEN the recommendation is repair. These rules form the knowledge base of the expert system.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The flowchart has three decision diamonds in a logical order, and every route ends in a recommendation with an accurate IF-THEN rule drawn from the scenario's values.

sampleAnswers.answer: IF the machine is five years old or more THEN recommend replacement. A younger machine is then checked against the repair quote.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One accurate IF-THEN rule is written and the younger-machine route is outlined, but no flowchart is constructed and the third decision is missing.

sampleAnswers.answer: IF the machine is old THEN replace it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One relevant rule is given without a flowchart, and 'old' is not defined, so the system could not test the condition.

prompts.question: Assess whether a knowledge base of IF-THEN rules drawn from a flowchart is a suitable design for the repair shop, considering how rules can conflict and how staff would maintain them.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: the repair shop plans to add rules for dishwashers and dryers over the next year. Two staff members have proposed different rules for the same fault, and the shop manager needs a knowledge base that people without programming skills can check and update.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the suitability of a flowchart-based knowledge base for the shop, weighing its clarity and checkability against the risk of conflicting rules and the effort of maintenance, and reaching a supported overall judgement
5 marks: Assesses the design with reference to rule conflicts or maintenance, with a sound reasoned judgement, but one of these factors is only briefly developed
4 marks: Discusses one strength and one weakness of the design for the shop, linked to the scenario, without a clear overall judgement
3 marks: Identifies one strength or one weakness of the design, with a brief link to the shop's needs
2 marks: Describes a flowchart or a rule in general terms, with no link to the shop
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported statement about knowledge bases
markerNotes: Assess needs a judgement on suitability, weighing the strengths of the design against the conflict and maintenance problems in the scenario.
The conflict between the two proposed rules is the scenario's clue, so a strong answer names a method for resolving conflicts, such as a priority order.
Maintenance points should be specific, such as checking each new rule against the existing ones.
commonStudentErrors: Describing what a flowchart is without judging whether it suits the repair shop.
Saying conflicts can be avoided simply by careful writing, without a method to resolve them.
Overlooking maintenance, or treating it as the same thing as writing the rules.

sampleAnswers.answer: A knowledge base of IF-THEN rules drawn from a flowchart, used by an expert system, is a suitable design for the shop in several respects. Each rule can be read and checked by staff without programming skills, and the flowchart shows the order of questions, which makes the logic transparent. However, two staff members proposing different rules for the same fault show the main weakness: rules can conflict, and a rule base with no priority order may give two recommendations for one machine. The shop would need to decide which rule takes precedence and record that decision in the knowledge base. Maintaining the rules is also a cost, because each new appliance adds rules that interact with existing ones, so every change needs a check for conflicts. The flowchart helps here because it can be redrawn and reviewed as a whole. On balance, the design suits a shop that adds rules slowly and reviews them each time, but it is not sufficient on its own, because the shop needs a clear conflict-resolution rule and a named person to maintain the knowledge base.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer weighs the clarity of the design against the conflict and maintenance problems, names a conflict-resolution method, and reaches a supported overall judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: A flowchart makes the rules easy to check, so staff without programming skills can follow them. However, two rules for the same fault may conflict, so the shop needs an order of priority.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One strength and one weakness are identified with a link to the shop, but the answer does not reach an overall judgement on suitability.

sampleAnswers.answer: A knowledge base of rules is useful for a repair shop.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant but unsupported statement is made. Assess the design against the conflict and maintenance problems in the scenario.

dotPoints.description: Design and model an automated smart system using a range of inputs and outputs

prompts.question: Identify one input sensor and one output actuator for an automated smart home security light.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A homeowner wants a porch light that switches on automatically when someone approaches the front door after dark. The light should turn off after a few minutes, without the homeowner needing to switch it on by hand.
markerNotes: An actuator acts on the environment (a relay, motor or valve), while a sensor measures it. Name the device that performs the function, not just the appliance.
Give the specific device type, such as a PIR motion sensor, rather than the general category 'sensor'.
Choose devices that fit the scenario: the security light needs to detect movement and to switch the light's power.
commonStudentErrors: Naming the light itself as the actuator, without the switching device (such as a relay) that the controller uses.
Naming a timer or switch as the input sensor, when it does not sense the environment.
Giving a general category such as 'sensor' or 'motor' without the specific device.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies one suitable input sensor (for example, a PIR motion sensor) and one suitable output actuator (for example, a relay that powers the light), each matched to the function it performs in the smart light system
1 mark: Identifies a suitable input sensor or output actuator, but not both, or names a device whose role is unclear

sampleAnswers.answer: The input sensor is a PIR sensor, which performs motion detection by sensing body heat. The output actuator is a relay that gives automated control of the security light when the smart system receives a signal from the sensor.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: a specific input sensor and an output actuator are named, and each is matched to its function in the smart light. Brief descriptions like these are the right length for a two-mark question.

sampleAnswers.answer: The input sensor is a motion sensor and the output is the light.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A suitable sensor is named, but the light is named as the output rather than the switching device that acts on it. Name the relay or switch as the actuator and explain that it powers the light when the sensor is triggered.

prompts.question: Construct a model for an automated smart window blind system for a home office, including the inputs, the processing logic and the outputs required for the system to operate intelligently.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A homeowner works from a home office that receives strong afternoon sun. She wants the window blinds to open and close automatically to manage light, glare and room temperature without her needing to adjust them.
markerNotes: A model needs three linked parts: inputs (what the system senses), processing logic (IF-THEN rules or an algorithm), and outputs (the actuator that acts).
Choose inputs that fit the purpose (light and temperature for glare and heat, time for schedules) and give a reason for each.
Logic with explicit thresholds and conditions can be tested, which earns more than a general statement such as 'close when hot'.
commonStudentErrors: Listing inputs and outputs without connecting them through processing logic.
Using vague logic such as 'if it is sunny, close the blinds', without a threshold or time condition.
Writing rules that conflict, such as opening and closing the blinds under the same conditions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Constructs a complete, coherent model: at least two relevant inputs (for example, a light sensor, a real-time clock and a temperature sensor) with their purpose; an output (a motor that opens and closes the blinds); and processing logic of IF-THEN rules that connect the inputs to the output in a testable, sensible way matched to the office's needs, such as heat and glare. The parts work together as one system
4 marks: Constructs a model with at least two inputs, an output and processing logic, with one part less complete or less clearly connected
3 marks: Identifies the inputs and output and gives some processing logic, but the logic is general or does not connect the inputs to the output clearly
2 marks: Identifies inputs or the output, with the processing logic absent or incomplete
1 mark: Names one input or the output, with no model or logic

sampleAnswers.answer:
This automated smart system for blinds would have three inputs and one output, with rules in the microcontroller that connect them.

**Inputs:**
1. A light sensor (photodiode) to measure the brightness of the sunlight outside the window.
2. A real-time clock to know the time of day.
3. An indoor temperature sensor to measure the heat in the room.

**Outputs:**
1. An actuator: a geared DC motor, driven by a motor controller, that raises and lowers the blinds.

**Processing logic:** The microcontroller would run these rules:
*   IF time is between 7am and 9am AND light_reading > threshold_A, THEN open the blinds to admit morning light.
*   IF time is after 9am AND light_reading > threshold_A AND room_temperature > 24°C, THEN close the blinds to reduce heat and glare.
*   IF light_reading < threshold_B, THEN close the blinds for privacy once it becomes dark.

Thresholds are set during testing to suit the room.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the model has inputs with a stated purpose, an output that moves the blinds, and testable IF-THEN logic that connects them. Setting thresholds during testing makes the processing logic operational, and the answer does that.

sampleAnswers.answer: Inputs: a light sensor and a clock. Output: a motor that moves the blinds. Logic: if it is sunny, close the blinds, and if it is evening, open them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The inputs and output are named and some logic is given, but the logic is too general to test and does not combine the time and temperature inputs. Write rules with explicit thresholds and conditions, and add a temperature input to address heat.

sampleAnswers.answer: The system needs a light sensor to measure how bright the sun is.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One input is named, but there is no output, no processing logic and no model of how the system decides. Add the motor that moves the blinds and the rules that determine when it acts.

dotPoints.description: Implement automated processing using software

prompts.question: Demonstrate, using short pseudocode, how software could automatically flag every product whose quantity on hand is below its reorder level, so that the owner does not check each row by hand.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a bicycle shop keeps its stock in a spreadsheet with columns for product code, quantity on hand and reorder level. The owner wants the software to run each morning and flag every product that needs ordering.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Demonstrates a correct, sequenced pseudocode routine that loops through every row, tests quantity against reorder level and flags each product, and explains clearly how the software runs without manual checking
3 marks: Demonstrates a correct routine with a loop or condition and a flag, but the explanation of automatic running is incomplete or the pseudocode omits one step
2 marks: Describes an IF test that flags low stock, with a general reference to software, but without a loop or a complete routine
1 mark: Names software or a spreadsheet function with no routine or test shown
markerNotes: Pseudocode needs a loop, a test and an output; a description of what the software could do earns less.
The automatic running, such as a scheduled morning trigger, is what makes the processing automated rather than manual.
Use the scenario's column names in the pseudocode to show that the routine fits the sheet.
commonStudentErrors: Writing a single IF test without a loop, so that only one product is checked.
Describing the spreadsheet's appearance rather than the logic that flags each row.
Forgetting that the process must run without manual checking, and so omitting how it is triggered.

sampleAnswers.answer:
This automated processing uses a loop and an IF test. The pseudocode is:
FOR each product row in the stock sheet
    IF quantity on hand < reorder level THEN
        set status to 'Reorder' and flag the row
    END IF
END FOR
The software runs this routine each morning, triggered on a schedule, so no one checks the rows by hand. The flagged rows can be filtered into a single list for the owner to order from, which keeps the process consistent and fast.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The pseudocode loops through every row, tests quantity against reorder level, and flags each product, and the answer explains how the software runs without manual checking.

sampleAnswers.answer: IF the quantity is below the reorder level THEN flag the product. The software checks each row in turn.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A correct IF test and flag are shown, but the routine has no explicit loop over every row and the automatic running is not described, which earns the middle band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The software could flag products that need reordering.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant function is named, but no routine or test is shown, so the answer cannot earn more than the bottom band.

prompts.question: Recommend whether the bicycle shop should automate its reorder process with a spreadsheet macro or a purchased stock-management package, given the owner's limited technical skills and the cost of ongoing maintenance.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: the bicycle shop owner has basic spreadsheet skills and a small annual budget. The stock sheet already records quantity on hand and each product's reorder level, and the owner wants reorder warnings to be generated automatically.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Recommends a reasoned choice between a spreadsheet macro and a purchased package, weighing the owner's technical skills, cost and maintenance needs, and justifying the recommendation with specific, relevant reasons
4 marks: Recommends one option with reasons that address the owner's skills or cost, but the maintenance trade-off is only briefly considered
3 marks: Compares the two options on one relevant factor, such as cost or the risk of breakage, but does not reach a recommendation
2 marks: Describes one option in general terms, with a simple advantage or disadvantage and no link to the owner's needs
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported statement about automation
markerNotes: Recommend means choosing one option and justifying it, weighing the owner's skills, cost and maintenance.
Maintenance is the scenario's key cost, so an answer that names it and weighs it earns more than one that discusses features alone.
A recommendation that includes a safeguard, such as a quarterly review, shows the judgement a top answer needs.
commonStudentErrors: Listing features of macros and packages without making a recommendation.
Recommending the package because it looks more professional, without considering the owner's budget or skills.
Ignoring the maintenance cost of a macro and treating it as a one-off build.

sampleAnswers.answer: A spreadsheet macro suits this shop because the stock sheet already exists and the owner has basic skills, so the automated processing can be built and changed at little extra cost. The macro can compare quantity on hand with each reorder level and flag products each morning, using the spreadsheet software the shop already has. However, a macro needs maintenance: if a column is moved or renamed, the code can stop working without warning, and the owner would have to repair it. A purchased stock-management package includes support and is less likely to break, but it costs more each year and requires staff time to learn. Given the owner's limited technical skills and small budget, the shop should adopt a simple, well-documented macro, reviewed each quarter, with the reorder level kept in a clearly labelled column.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer makes a reasoned recommendation, weighs the owner's skills and budget against the maintenance trade-off, and adds a safeguard that shows judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: A spreadsheet macro is cheaper, but it may break if the sheet's columns change, whereas a package includes support. The owner should weigh cost against the risk of breakage.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The two options are compared on cost and breakage, but no recommendation is reached, which limits the answer to the middle band.

sampleAnswers.answer: A macro could flag stock automatically.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant point about automation is made, but it is not compared with the package and no recommendation is given.

dotPoints.description: Assess the output produced by a decision support system, including graphing to detail the success of decisions, and comparing the proposed versus the actual outputs

prompts.question: Calculate the percentage of proposed orders that were within 10 per cent of actual demand, and calculate the difference in units for the product described, showing your working.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a bicycle shop's decision support system proposed 50 stock orders in one month, and 38 of those orders were within 10 per cent of actual demand. For one product, the system proposed an order of 120 units, but actual demand was 150 units.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Calculates both the percentage of orders within 10 per cent of demand (76 per cent) and the product's difference (30 units under-ordered), showing working, and interprets what the results suggest about the system's output
3 marks: Calculates both values correctly with working shown for one of them, and makes a brief interpretation of the results
2 marks: Calculates one value correctly with working, or both values without interpretation
1 mark: Calculates one value correctly with no working or interpretation
markerNotes: Show each calculation with its numbers; a correct answer with no working earns less than one that shows the steps.
Percentages should use the right base, such as the 50 orders or the actual demand, and the base should be stated.
Interpretation matters: say what the results suggest about the system, such as under-ordering a product.
commonStudentErrors: Calculating 38 ÷ 50 but giving the answer as 0.76 without converting it to a percentage.
Dividing the difference by the proposed order instead of the actual demand, which gives the wrong base.
Reporting the difference as 30 units without saying whether the system over- or under-ordered.

sampleAnswers.answer: Orders within 10 per cent of actual demand: 38 of 50 proposed orders, so the percentage is 38 ÷ 50 × 100 = 76 per cent. For the product, the difference is 150 − 120 = 30 units, so the proposed order was below the actual output by 30 units. As a share of actual demand, that is 30 ÷ 150 × 100 = 20 per cent. The decision support system has a success rate of 76 per cent, which is useful but not reliable, and it under-ordered this product by 20 per cent, suggesting it underestimated demand.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both values are calculated with working, the base for each percentage is stated, and the results are interpreted in terms of the system's output.

sampleAnswers.answer: The success rate is 38 out of 50, which is 76 per cent. The product's difference is 30 units.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both values are correct, but no working or interpretation is given, so the answer earns the middle band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The difference for the product is 30 units.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One value is calculated correctly, with no working and no interpretation.

prompts.question: Discuss how a graph of proposed against actual outputs over twelve months can show whether a decision support system's decisions are improving, and what such a graph cannot show about why some decisions failed.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a bicycle shop's decision support system has produced a stock order each month for a year. The owner plots proposed orders against actual sales on one line graph and wants to know whether the system's decisions are getting more accurate.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses how the graph shows change in the gap between proposed and actual outputs over time, and what it cannot reveal about causes, with reasoned links to the owner's question
4 marks: Discusses the graph's use for showing trends in accuracy and at least one limitation, linked to the bicycle shop, but the limitation is briefly explained
3 marks: Describes what the graph shows about proposed and actual outputs, with one limitation stated but not developed
2 marks: Describes the graph in general terms, with no limitation and no link to the owner's question
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported statement about graphs or outputs
markerNotes: Discuss requires weighing what the graph reveals against what it cannot reveal, not describing the graph alone.
Use the bicycle shop example, such as a supplier delay, to show what the graph cannot reveal about causes.
The strongest answers explain how to close the gap in the evidence, such as recording the data used for each order.
commonStudentErrors: Describing how to draw a line graph without saying what it shows about the system's accuracy.
Claiming the graph proves the system is learning, when the graph shows only the size of the gap.
Naming a limitation without explaining why it matters for the owner's question.

sampleAnswers.answer: A line graph with proposed and actual output on the same axes shows the gap each month, so the owner can see whether the gap narrows over the year. If the actual line moves closer to the proposed line, the decision support system is becoming more accurate, and the graph shows the size of each error in units. However, the graph cannot show why an individual decision failed. A month of low sales may reflect a local event, a supplier delay or a poor input to the forecast, and the graph shows only that the outputs differed. It also cannot show whether a decision was right for the wrong reason, or whether one unusual month distorts the picture. The owner should therefore record the data used for each order alongside the graph, so that decisions can be checked against their inputs as well as their results.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer shows how the graph reveals change in accuracy over time, then weighs what it cannot reveal about causes, and closes the gap with a practical step.

sampleAnswers.answer: The graph shows whether the gap between proposed and actual outputs is shrinking. However, it does not explain why a particular order was wrong.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The graph's use is described and one limitation is stated, but the limitation is not developed and no link to the owner's question is made.

sampleAnswers.answer: The graph shows the proposed and actual orders.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant but unsupported statement is made, with no discussion of what the graph shows or what it cannot show.

dotPoints.description: Explain how expert systems contribute to the efficiency of intelligent systems (supercomputers; digital assistants; autonomous vehicles; streaming services)

prompts.question: Outline how an expert system contributes to the efficiency of a media streaming service.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A streaming service has millions of subscribers, and each viewer wants to find something to watch quickly. The service's recommendations are rule-based, using what each viewer has watched and the features of each title.
markerNotes: Outline means brief points: connect the expert system directly to the efficiency gain, such as less searching and faster matching.
The rules must use inputs the system has, such as viewing history, genre, actors and ratings.
The answer is about a rule-based expert system, so describe the rules and inference rather than machine learning.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the recommendations as 'AI' without showing the rules, the knowledge base or the inference.
Stating that it is 'faster' without saying what makes it faster, such as matching rules to viewing data rather than the viewer searching manually.
Confusing the expert system with the user interface that displays the recommendations.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Outlines clearly how the expert system works (a knowledge base of rules linking viewing history and content features, applied by an inference engine) and states the efficiency gain, which is quicker discovery of relevant content and higher engagement
1 mark: Identifies a recommendation feature, or states an efficiency benefit, without explaining how the expert system achieves it

sampleAnswers.answer: An expert system in a streaming service works as a rule-based recommendation engine. Its knowledge base links viewing history and content features to rules, and its inference engine filters the catalogue, which improves efficiency by reducing search time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the expert system is outlined as a knowledge base of rules and an inference engine, and the efficiency gain is stated as less search time for viewers. The answer stays focused on the expert system itself, which is what the question asks.

sampleAnswers.answer: An expert system recommends shows to users.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The recommendation function is named, but the efficiency benefit is not stated and the rules and inference behind it are not explained. Explain how the system uses rules on viewing history and content features, and what this saves the viewer or the service.

prompts.question: Explain how multiple expert systems work together within an autonomous vehicle to contribute to its overall safety and efficiency.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: An autonomous vehicle is navigating a busy city street with traffic lights, pedestrians and other cars nearby. Its sensors feed several expert systems that must interpret the environment and decide how to drive safely.
markerNotes: Explain at least two systems, each with its own knowledge base of rules, and show how the output of one (facts) feeds the inference engine of the other.
Name the vehicle functions the systems support (perceiving objects; planning and deciding a path) and link each to safety or efficiency.
Use concrete rules as examples, but note that real vehicles combine rule-based logic with machine-learning classifiers.
commonStudentErrors: Describing only one expert system and calling it several, without a second system's rules and inference.
Saying the car 'uses AI' without explaining knowledge bases, rules or inference.
Explaining safety but not efficiency, although the question asks for both.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains clearly two or more interacting expert systems, for example a perception system that turns sensor data into facts such as 'pedestrian ahead', and a path-planning system whose knowledge base holds road rules and vehicle limits. Explains how the output of one feeds the inference engine of the other in a continuous loop, and how this makes the vehicle both safe and efficient, with accurate, specific examples of rules
5 marks: Explains two expert systems and their interaction, with the link to safety and efficiency less fully developed, or one system briefly explained
4 marks: Explains two systems with a clear role each, but the interaction between them is not clearly developed
3 marks: Describes the role of one expert system in the vehicle, with a general reference to others
2 marks: Identifies sensors or planning in general terms, without explaining the expert system's rules and reasoning
1 mark: Names an expert system or a vehicle function with no explanation

sampleAnswers.answer:
An autonomous vehicle is a complex intelligent system that relies on several specialised expert systems working together.

One critical component is the **perception system**. This expert system takes data from sensors such as cameras and LiDAR and uses a knowledge base of rules to identify and classify objects. For example, a simplified rule might be 'IF an object has a human shape AND is located on the footpath or at the kerb, THEN classify it as a pedestrian'. Real vehicles often use machine-learning classifiers for this task, but the rule shows the expert-system logic. This turns raw sensor data into meaningful facts.

These facts are passed to a second **path planning and decision-making system**. Its knowledge base contains the rules of the road, principles of defensive driving and the vehicle's physical limitations. Its inference engine uses the facts from the perception system (for example, 'there is a pedestrian ahead') to make efficient, safe decisions such as 'decrease speed' or 'change lanes'.

These systems work together in a continuous loop. The perception system constantly updates the facts about the environment, and the planning system constantly reassesses its decisions, which is what allows the vehicle to drive with both safety and efficiency in a dynamic environment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: two expert systems are explained with their knowledge bases, the facts that pass between them, and the inference that turns those facts into safe, efficient decisions. The concrete example rule shows the expert-system logic clearly, and the note on machine learning keeps it accurate.

sampleAnswers.answer: The vehicle has a perception system that uses sensors to identify objects, such as pedestrians and traffic lights. It passes this information to a path planning system, which uses rules about road laws to choose a safe route. Together, the two systems help the car drive safely and efficiently.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two expert systems are identified with clear roles, but the rules and inference that connect the facts to decisions are not explained, and the interaction between the systems is only stated. Give an example rule in the planning system and explain how the facts from perception drive its inference.

sampleAnswers.answer: A self-driving car has sensors and a computer that makes driving decisions. An expert system can stop the car when a pedestrian is detected.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer is general and describes one function without explaining the rules or reasoning of either system. Describe the perception system and the path-planning system separately, including the rules each one uses.

dotPoints.description: Describe the tools and processes used to manage and document the development of an enterprise system (problem definition; time and resource management, including Gantt charts; an iterative approach; production process and technical skills; testing and evaluation)

prompts.question: Identify one tool used for time management and one process used for project development.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A project manager at a software company is beginning to plan a new customer records system. The project has a fixed launch date, and the team must agree on how it will manage its time and build the system.
markerNotes: Identify two different things, a time management tool and a development process, and name each clearly.
A short description (what the Gantt chart shows, or what an iterative cycle involves) earns more than a bare name.
A process is a method for building the system, not a document or a single phase of work.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a general tool, such as a spreadsheet, without saying how it manages time.
Naming two tools when the question asks for one time management tool and one development process.
Naming a single phase, such as testing, as a development process.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies a suitable time management tool (for example, a Gantt chart showing tasks, durations and dependencies) and a suitable development process (for example, an iterative approach), with a brief statement of what each does
1 mark: Identifies one suitable tool or process only, or names two items from the same category

sampleAnswers.answer: A tool used for time management is a Gantt chart, which visually represents the project schedule. A process used for project development is an iterative approach, where the project is built in repeated cycles of development and testing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: a suitable time management tool and a development process are each named, with a short description of what each does. This is the right length for a two-mark identification question.

sampleAnswers.answer: A Gantt chart is a tool used to show the timing of tasks in a project.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A suitable time management tool is named and described, but no development process is identified. Add a process such as an iterative approach or agile methodology and say briefly what it involves.

prompts.question: Describe how an iterative approach and a Gantt chart are used to manage the development of a new enterprise system.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A software development team is building a customer relationship management (CRM) system for a large company. The company wants the system delivered in stages, so the team must plan its time and track progress against a fixed timeline.
markerNotes: Describe both tools in the context of managing development: iterations for flexible delivery, and the Gantt chart for scheduling tasks and dependencies.
The top marks lie in linking the two: the Gantt chart plans and tracks the tasks inside each iteration.
Use the CRM scenario, for example iterations for the customer module before the reporting module, to make the description specific.
commonStudentErrors: Describing an iterative approach as building the whole system at once, or as the same as a waterfall approach.
Describing a Gantt chart only as a 'picture of the schedule', without tasks, durations, dependencies or milestones.
Describing the two tools separately, with no link between them.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Describes both tools and how they work together: the iterative approach builds the system in repeated cycles of planning, design, building and testing, with feedback between cycles; the Gantt chart shows tasks, durations, dependencies and milestones, and is used to schedule and track each iteration against the overall timeline and resources. Uses the CRM scenario to link them accurately
4 marks: Describes both tools clearly, with the link between them less developed or the scenario link weak
3 marks: Describes one tool in detail and the other briefly, or describes both with general features only
2 marks: Describes the iterative approach or the Gantt chart accurately, with limited detail
1 mark: Names either tool with minimal description

sampleAnswers.answer:
An iterative approach is a process where the enterprise system is developed in a series of repeated cycles or 'iterations'. In each cycle, a small portion of the system is designed, built, and tested. This allows the development team to get regular feedback from the client and make adjustments, which is more flexible than building the entire system at once.

A Gantt chart is a project management tool used for time and resource management. It is a horizontal bar chart that visually displays the project schedule. It lists all required tasks, their start and end dates, their durations, and their dependencies (which tasks must be completed before others can begin). The team would use the Gantt chart to plan the specific tasks and allocate resources for each iteration, and to track progress against the project's overall timeline and deadlines.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the iterative approach is described as repeated cycles with feedback, the Gantt chart's features are specific, and the answer links the two in the context of the CRM project. That link is what separates a five-mark answer from two separate descriptions.

sampleAnswers.answer: An iterative approach builds the system in parts, and each part is tested before the next one starts. A Gantt chart is a chart that shows the tasks on a timeline, so the team can see when each task is due.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both tools are described in general terms, and the answer does not link them or refer to the CRM system. Explain the repeated cycles of an iterative approach, and show how the Gantt chart's tasks, dependencies and milestones are used to plan each iteration.

sampleAnswers.answer: A Gantt chart is used to show the timeline of a project.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Only the chart is described, with a single function, and the iterative approach is not mentioned. Describe the cycles of the iterative approach and how the team uses the Gantt chart within them.

dotPoints.description: Explain the effect of the changing nature of enterprise on the development of projects (offshore development; working remotely; freelance work; enabling the growth of start-ups)

prompts.question: Identify one benefit and one challenge of using offshore development for a project.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: An Australian company is considering hiring a software development team in another country to build its customer portal. Managers want to know the main advantage and the main difficulty before they sign a contract.
markerNotes: Give one benefit and one challenge, each specific to offshore development: cost or talent access for the benefit, and time zones, communication or quality control for the challenge.
A reason for each, such as lower wages for similar skills, shows understanding beyond the label.
A challenge should be specific to working across distance, not a general project risk.
commonStudentErrors: Listing two benefits, such as cost and talent, when the question asks for one benefit and one challenge.
Presenting cost savings as guaranteed, without noting that coordination and management costs can offset them.
Naming 'risk' or 'problems' without identifying what the challenge is.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies one valid benefit (for example, lower labour costs or access to a wider talent pool) and one valid challenge (for example, time zone differences, communication barriers or quality control), each with a brief reason
1 mark: Identifies one valid benefit or one valid challenge only, or lists two benefits or two challenges

sampleAnswers.answer: A benefit of offshore development for an enterprise is often a significant reduction in labour costs. A challenge is managing communication and collaboration effectively across different time zones and cultural contexts.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: one benefit and one challenge are given, each with a reason. The answer is concise and specific to offshore development, which is what a two-mark identification question asks for.

sampleAnswers.answer: A benefit of offshore development is that it can be cheaper than hiring locally.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A benefit is named, but no challenge is given, and the cost point needs a reason. Add one challenge, such as time zone differences or communication barriers, and say briefly why it matters for the project.

prompts.question: Explain how the trends of 'working remotely' and the growth of 'freelance work' have affected how enterprise projects are resourced and managed.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A technology start-up needs a small team to build a new mobile application on a limited budget. It is deciding whether to hire remote staff and freelancers, rather than full-time employees, for each part of the project.
markerNotes: Explain the effect on both resourcing (who is hired, from where and for how long) and management (coordination, outcomes and contracts).
Use the start-up scenario: a small team, a new product and a limited budget make the points about flexibility and cost concrete.
Name a type of tool or practice, such as online collaboration boards, outcome-based goals or defined contracts, rather than 'technology'.
commonStudentErrors: Describing remote working as 'people working from home' without explaining the effect on resourcing and management.
Saying freelancers are always cheaper or always less reliable, without noting the need for clear contracts and well-defined tasks.
Confusing freelance work, which is an employment arrangement, with offshore development, which is about where the work is done.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains clearly how remote working and freelance work have changed the resourcing and management of enterprise projects. Remote work widens the talent pool and needs online collaboration tools and outcome-focused management; freelance work gives access to specialised skills on a flexible, as-needed basis but requires clear tasks, contracts and coordination. Shows the trade-offs and links both to the start-up scenario
3 marks: Explains both trends accurately, with the management implications or trade-offs developed for only one
2 marks: Explains one trend in some detail, or describes both trends in general terms
1 mark: Names remote work or freelance work with a general effect

sampleAnswers.answer:
Working remotely means enterprise projects are no longer limited by geography when sourcing talent. It requires heavy reliance on online collaboration tools such as Slack, Zoom and Jira, and project management must focus on clear documentation and measurable outcomes across a distributed team.

Freelance work has changed resourcing by letting enterprises, especially start-ups, access highly specialised skills for specific parts of a project without hiring full-time staff. A project might hire a freelance UI designer for two months. This is cost-effective, but it requires managers to break the project into discrete tasks and manage contracts carefully.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: both trends are explained, covering the effect on resourcing (a wider talent pool, specialised skills on demand) and on management (outcomes, coordination and contracts), all linked to the start-up. Naming the trade-offs is what moves the answer into the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Working remotely means a company can hire people from anywhere, so it needs tools such as video calls to stay in contact. Freelance workers can be hired for particular tasks, which saves money on full-time staff.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both trends are described in general terms: the benefit and a tool are named, but the change to management style and the need for clear contracts and well-defined tasks are not explained. Explain how managers focus on outcomes and define tasks for freelancers to reach 3 or 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Freelance work means people are hired for short jobs on a project.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One trend is described with a general effect, and remote working is not addressed. Explain how remote working changes the way the team is managed and coordinated.

dotPoints.description: Investigate tools that support the design and development of an enterprise system (online collaboration; time/task action plans; process diary, including ongoing evaluation; budget; system flowcharts; data flow diagrams; decision trees)

prompts.question: Distinguish between a system flowchart and a data flow diagram (DFD).
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A systems analyst at a small training college is documenting how a proposed online enrolment system will work. The analyst needs to show the sequence of steps for students and the movement of enrolment data between the system's parts.
markerNotes: Distinguish by focus: a system flowchart shows the sequence of steps and decisions (control flow), while a DFD shows how data moves between sources, processes and stores.
Use the terms accurately: a DFD has external entities, processes, data flows and data stores, while a flowchart uses start, process, decision and end symbols.
A difference stated as what each diagram shows earns more than a statement that both are diagrams.
